claims.text: Integrating high-throughput calorimetry with first-principles modeling enables accurate determination of melting temperature across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The integrated approach enables accurate determination of enthalpy and entropy of fusion across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The integrated approach enables accurate determination of volume change at melting across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The integrated approach enables accurate determination of liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The proposed integrated approach is efficient or high-throughput.
The intended samples are well-homogenized, single-phase high-entropy alloys spanning fcc, bcc, and hcp structures.
DSC and dilatometry under controlled atmosphere can be combined with Monte Carlo and DFT-based simulations for the proposed measurements.
DFT calculations can connect local cation disorder or intermixing with lattice stabilization.
Atomic-scale crystal-ordering fluctuations occur in high-entropy or complex-concentrated alloy systems.
High configurational entropy affects the structure and dynamics of supercooled high-entropy metallic liquids and glasses.
Simulations incorporating configurational entropy and ordering fluctuations can correct DSC-derived fusion data for non-ideal mixing.
Accounting for configurational entropy and subtle ordering changes improves predictions of fusion-related properties.
Melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change will agree with model predictions within approximately 5–10%.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties will agree with model predictions within approximately 10–15%.
Traditional DSC and dilatometry without computational corrections have larger uncertainties and fail to fully capture configurational and structural fluctuations.
The approach should perform best for stable, single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
Multiphase alloys and systems with pronounced segregation require additional modeling refinements.
A CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy can exhibit Cu segregation in its cast base-metal microstructure and reduced microsegregation in a laser-welded fusion zone.
Performance remains uncertain for alloys with extreme compositional disparities or unforeseen phase instabilities.
Consistent experimental-model deviations exceeding 15% in a statistically significant alloy set, or absence of the expected ordering and configurational-entropy trends, would falsify the approach.
